summary: This proposed standard defines MIB objects for managing the Link Control Protocol and Link Quality Monitoring on interfaces that use the Point-to-Point Protocol family.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP connects two computers over a line. This paper lists what a network manager can check about how that connection is set up and how good it is.

questions: snmp objects for ppp link control
what is the ppp lcp mib
what is ppp link quality monitoring
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring PPP links, their quality reports and two built-in link tests.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to see and configure how Point-to-Point Protocol links are set up and how well they are performing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module, PPP-LCP-MIB, with a mandatory Link group, an LQR group for link quality reports, an optional LQR Extensions group, and two tests, Echo and Discard.
tldr.outcome: Managers get tables of status and configuration per PPP interface, tied into the standard interface table, with configuration separated so it can be protected.

today: RFC 1471 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the SNMP framework of RFC 1157 and the PPP specification of RFC 1331.

sections.title: The Management Framework and Selection Criteria
sections.content:
The memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for TCP/IP network management. It fits the Internet-standard framework: the SMI (RFC 1155) for naming objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) for core objects and SNMP (RFC 1157) for access. Objects are defined with a subset of ASN.1 and named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER.

To keep the MIB simple, objects had to be essential for fault or configuration management, show evidence of use, be few in number and not be derivable from other objects. Objects whose sole purpose was to debug implementations were excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors only included gauges that a manager really needs. They left out ones that were just for people building the software.

sections.title: How PPP Is Modeled
sections.content:
PPP is not one protocol but a family. The RFC groups it into three categories. Control Protocols run PPP itself and include the Link Control Protocol (LCP), PAP, Link Quality Report (LQR) and CHAP. Network Protocols carry the traffic of a higher-layer protocol over the link. Network Control Protocols (NCPs) control each Network Protocol, for example IP Control Protocol for IP.

This document covers only the objects for managing LCP and Link Quality Monitoring.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is like a team: some members set up the line, some carry the messages, and some manage the carriers. This paper is about the ones that set up the line and check how good it is.

sections.title: MIB Groups and the Interface Table
sections.content:
Groups are the unit of conformance: if a group applies to an implementation, all its objects must be implemented. The PPP Link Group is mandatory for all PPP implementations. The PPP LQR Group is mandatory for implementations that implement LQR. The PPP LQR Extensions Group is optional. Each of the first two has a status table and a configuration table, and the configuration table is separate so it can be placed in a different MIB view for security.

The PPP MIB extends the standard interface group. A PPP interface has a single entry in the ifTable, and pppLinkStatusPhysicalIndex holds the ifIndex of the lower-layer interface such as an RS-232 port. Setting ifAdminStatus to up or down injects an administrative open or close event into the LCP state machine. ifOperStatus is up when the state machine is in the Opened state. A linkUp trap should be sent on reaching Opened and a linkDown trap on leaving it.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges come in bundles. One bundle is required for every PPP line. Another is only for lines that check their quality. The settings are kept apart so they can be locked away.

sections.title: The PPP Link Group
sections.content:
The status table has counters for bad packets, all of which count toward ifInErrors: pppLinkStatusBadAddresses, pppLinkStatusBadControls, pppLinkStatusPacketTooLongs and pppLinkStatusBadFCSs. It also shows the negotiated values for each direction: MRU, ACC map, protocol compression, address and control compression and FCS size. These are meaningful only once the link is open, when ifOperStatus is up.

The configuration table holds the initial settings, which take effect when the link is next restarted: pppLinkConfigInitialMRU (default 1500, 0 means advertise none), the receive and transmit ACC maps (default ffffffff hex), pppLinkConfigMagicNumber (default false) and pppLinkConfigFcsSize (default 16 bits). The local node always complies with negotiations started by the remote node.
sections.plainLanguage: One gauge counts broken messages. Others show what the two ends agreed on, such as the biggest message size. Dials let the manager pick starting choices for the next time the line restarts.

sections.title: Link Quality Reports and Tests
sections.content:
The LQR group has an entry for a link only if Link Quality Monitoring was successfully negotiated. pppLqrQuality reports good, bad or not-determined, and the RFC does not define what good or bad means. Other objects give the LQR counters and the reporting periods, in hundredths of a second, for the local and remote sides. The config table sets the period to negotiate and enables or disables LQR negotiation.

The optional Extensions group stores the most recently received LQR packet, pppLqrExtnsLastReceivedLqrPacket, as 68 octets in network byte order. Keeping it gives a synchronized record of the counters, so external code can apply its own policy for declaring a link bad.

Two tests can be run through the interface test table: the Echo Test sends a PPP Echo Packet and succeeds if the response returns properly, and the Discard Test sends a Discard Packet and succeeds if it is transmitted without error. What counts as proper or an error is left to the implementor. Running them does not put the link in the testing state.
sections.plainLanguage: A quality gauge says good, bad or not sure. Two test buttons let the manager send a ping or a throwaway message down the line to see if it works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The PPP MIB lets an operator configure and control PPP links, which is a security risk. The RFC addresses it in three ways. Variables that carry significant risk are placed in separate, optional groups that an implementor may skip. Implementors may make risky variables read-only, though this is not recommended because authentication variables can still be read. With SNMPv2, the operator can put the variables in protected MIB views or make them inaccessible, and keeping security-related variables in separate tables makes that easier.
sections.plainLanguage: Because these dials can change how the line works, the risky ones are kept in separate boxes that can be locked or left out.
